Structure-based drug design uses crystal structures of target proteins to position inhibitors that fill specific pockets. The HIV protease inhibitors saquinavir, ritonavir, and the subsequent generation of darunavir all carry transition-state mimetic hydroxyethylamine or hydroxyethylene cores that occupy the catalytic dyad. Backbone hydrogen-bonding patterns rather than side-chain contacts give darunavir its retention of potency against resistance mutations that escape earlier drugs.

Cytochrome P450 enzymes oxidise drug molecules at the soft electrophilic positions through an iron-oxo intermediate, hydroxylating allylic and benzylic carbons, dealkylating N-methyl and O-methyl groups, and epoxidising electron-rich alkenes. CYP3A4 metabolises roughly half of marketed drugs, and inhibitors such as ketoconazole or grapefruit juice furanocoumarins raise plasma concentrations of co-administered substrates, often producing clinically important interactions.

Antibody-drug conjugates link a monoclonal antibody to a cytotoxic payload through a cleavable linker, delivering the cytotoxin selectively to antigen-expressing tumour cells. Trastuzumab emtansine combines the HER2-targeting antibody with the microtubule poison DM1 through a non-cleavable thioether linker; intracellular catabolism releases the lysine-DM1 metabolite. Drug-antibody ratio near 3.5 balances potency with pharmacokinetics, retained by judicious cysteine conjugation chemistry.

Covalent kinase inhibitors target a non-catalytic cysteine residue near the ATP-binding site through a Michael acceptor warhead such as an acrylamide. Ibrutinib forms an irreversible bond to Cys481 of Bruton's tyrosine kinase, prolonging the duration of target inhibition beyond the plasma half-life. Selectivity arises because most other kinases lack a cysteine at the analogous position; the few that share it constitute the off-target profile.

Fragment-based drug discovery starts from low-molecular-weight chemical fragments of 150 to 300 daltons that bind weakly at micromolar to millimolar affinity. Crystallography or NMR identifies the binding pose, and iterative growing or linking elaborates the fragment toward nanomolar affinity. Venetoclax, a BCL-2 inhibitor for chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, emerged from this strategy applied to the hydrophobic groove that normally accommodates BH3-only proteins.

Targeted protein degradation through PROTACs joins a target-binding ligand and an E3 ligase-recruiting moiety through a flexible linker. The resulting bifunctional molecule induces ternary complex formation between target, ligase, and PROTAC, leading to ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of the target. Catalytic mechanism of action and event-driven rather than occupancy-driven pharmacology give degraders advantages over conventional inhibitors of so-called undruggable scaffolding proteins.

Mercury cycling between atmosphere, ocean, and soil is dominated by the long lifetime of elemental Hg(0) in the gas phase, several months to a year, allowing global redistribution from emission sources. Oxidation to Hg(II) by bromine atoms in polar sunrise produces atmospheric mercury depletion events; deposited Hg(II) is methylated in sediments and bioaccumulates as methylmercury through the aquatic food web, biomagnifying by factors approaching 10^6 in top predators.

Persistent organic pollutants such as polychlorinated biphenyls, dioxins, and the legacy pesticide DDT resist biodegradation because of high carbon-chlorine bond strength and steric protection of the aromatic ring. Their octanol-water partition coefficients above 10^6 drive bioaccumulation in fatty tissue. The Stockholm Convention has phased out their production, yet legacy contamination in cold remote regions persists because volatilisation-condensation cycles distil them poleward over decades.

Nitrogen runoff from agricultural fertiliser enters waterways largely as nitrate. In eutrophic estuaries the excess nitrogen stimulates phytoplankton blooms whose decomposition consumes oxygen, producing hypoxic dead zones. The Gulf of Mexico dead zone fed by Mississippi River discharge varies between 5,000 and 20,000 square kilometres annually, with denitrification in shelf sediments releasing the nitrogen as N2 but also as the powerful greenhouse gas N2O.

Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances earn the name forever chemicals because their carbon-fluorine bonds resist hydrolysis, photolysis, and biological degradation. Perfluorooctanoic acid was detected in serum of essentially all sampled Americans by 2005, with environmental concentrations above the recently revised EPA drinking water health advisory of 0.004 parts per trillion. Atmospheric oxidation of fluorotelomer alcohols produces perfluorocarboxylic acids that deposit globally including in remote Arctic ecosystems.

Ocean acidification reduces seawater pH by approximately 0.1 unit since pre-industrial times as anthropogenic CO2 dissolves and shifts the carbonate equilibrium toward bicarbonate and protons. The calcium carbonate saturation state Omega decreases as carbonate ion concentration falls, threatening calcifying organisms once Omega drops below unity. Polar oceans, with naturally lower carbonate concentrations from cold-water solubility, will become undersaturated for aragonite first.

Arsenic contamination of groundwater in Bangladesh originates from reductive dissolution of arsenic-bearing iron oxyhydroxides under anoxic alluvial aquifer conditions. Concentrations exceeding the WHO guideline of 10 micrograms per litre affect tens of millions of people drinking from shallow tube wells. Co-precipitation with iron is the practical treatment: aeration oxidises As(III) to As(V), and Fe(III) flocs adsorb the arsenate, removing it from the water column.

Photochemical degradation of dissolved organic matter in surface waters is initiated by UV absorption that generates excited triplet states, singlet oxygen, hydroxyl radical, and superoxide. These reactive intermediates oxidise trace organic pollutants, photobleach the chromophoric component of dissolved organic matter, and influence the redox cycling of iron and manganese. Solar UV thereby provides a natural sink for hydrophobic contaminants in transparent oligotrophic waters.

Microplastic weathering in the marine environment proceeds through UV-induced chain scission of polyethylene and polypropylene, generating carbonyl groups detectable by FTIR. Brittle photo-oxidised fragments then crack into nanoplastics under wave action. The resulting particles adsorb hydrophobic pollutants from seawater up to a million-fold higher than ambient concentrations, providing a vector for pollutant uptake by filter-feeders that mistake the particles for food.

Soil cation exchange capacity quantifies the ability of negatively charged clay and humus surfaces to hold exchangeable cations such as Ca2+, Mg2+, K+, and NH4+. Sandy soils have CEC near 5 milliequivalents per 100 grams while montmorillonite-rich soils exceed 100. The CEC governs nutrient availability to plants and the retention of basic cations against leaching, a fundamental parameter in fertility assessment and remediation of cation-contaminated sites.

Chromium speciation determines toxicity in industrial effluents: Cr(III) is a poorly absorbed essential trace nutrient while Cr(VI) is a powerful oxidiser and known human carcinogen. Treatment of chromate-bearing wastewater proceeds by reduction with sodium sulphite or ferrous sulphate at low pH, followed by precipitation of Cr(OH)3 at pH 8 to 9. The amphoteric hydroxide redissolves above pH 11, narrowing the precipitation window.

A buffer prepared from 0.10 M acetic acid and 0.10 M sodium acetate resists pH change because added strong acid is consumed by the conjugate base and added strong base by the weak acid. The Henderson-Hasselbalch expression pH = pKa + log([A-]/[HA]) shows the pH equals the pKa of 4.76 when the two components are equimolar, and the buffer capacity is greatest within one pH unit of that value.

Polyprotic phosphoric acid dissociates in three steps with pKa values of 2.15, 7.20, and 12.35. Because successive constants differ by roughly five orders of magnitude, the titration curve shows two clear inflection points before the third proton, which is too weak to titrate cleanly in water. The wide separation lets a phosphate buffer be tuned across the physiological range near the second equivalence point.

The pH of a 0.010 M solution of the weak acid HA with Ka of 1.8e-5 is found by solving x squared divided by (0.010 minus x) equals Ka. The small-x approximation gives x near 4.2e-4, so the pH is about 3.4 and the degree of ionisation is only 4 percent, illustrating that weak acids deliver far fewer free protons than their formal concentration suggests.

At the equivalence point of a weak acid titrated with strong base, the solution contains only the conjugate base, so the pH is above 7. Hydrolysis of acetate, A- plus water giving HA plus hydroxide, has Kb equal to Kw divided by Ka. For 0.050 M acetate this yields a hydroxide concentration near 5.3e-6 M and a pH close to 8.7.

The autoionisation of water, expressed by Kw equal to the product of hydronium and hydroxide concentrations, equals 1.0e-14 at 25 degrees Celsius but rises to 9.3e-14 at 60 degrees because the process is endothermic. Consequently the neutral pH of pure water falls below 7 at elevated temperature, even though the solution remains exactly neutral with equal concentrations of the two ions.

Leveling occurs because any acid stronger than hydronium is fully converted to hydronium in water, so hydrochloric, perchloric, and nitric acids appear equally strong in aqueous solution. To rank their intrinsic strengths a less basic solvent such as glacial acetic acid is used, where differentiation reveals perchloric acid as the strongest of the common mineral acids.

The carbonic acid bicarbonate system buffers blood near pH 7.4. Dissolved carbon dioxide hydrates to carbonic acid, which dissociates to bicarbonate and a proton with an effective pKa of 6.1. The lungs adjust the carbon dioxide partial pressure and the kidneys adjust bicarbonate, so the open buffer operates far more effectively than a closed system fixed at its pKa would predict.

An amino acid such as glycine exists as a zwitterion at physiological pH, with a protonated ammonium group and a deprotonated carboxylate. The isoelectric point, where the net charge is zero, equals the average of the two relevant pKa values, 2.34 and 9.60, giving pI near 5.97. Below pI the molecule carries net positive charge and migrates toward the cathode in electrophoresis.

The inductive effect explains why trichloroacetic acid, with pKa 0.66, is far stronger than acetic acid at pKa 4.76. Three electronegative chlorine atoms withdraw electron density through the sigma framework, stabilising the carboxylate anion and shifting the dissociation equilibrium toward the ionised form. Each successive chlorine substitution lowers the pKa by roughly one to two units.

A solubility curve coupled to acid-base chemistry governs the dissolution of metal hydroxides. Aluminium hydroxide is amphoteric, dissolving in acid as the hexaaquo cation and in strong base as the tetrahydroxoaluminate anion. Its minimum solubility lies near pH 6 to 7, which is exploited in water treatment where flocculation of aluminium hydroxide sweeps suspended particulates from the supply.

A second-order reaction of the form 2A giving products has the integrated rate law 1 over [A] equals 1 over [A]0 plus 2kt. A plot of reciprocal concentration against time is linear with slope 2k, and the half-life 1 over (2k[A]0) lengthens as the reaction proceeds, in sharp contrast to a first-order process whose half-life remains constant throughout.

The steady-state approximation sets the net rate of change of a reactive intermediate to zero, allowing its concentration to be expressed in terms of stable species. Applied to the Lindemann mechanism for unimolecular decomposition, it predicts a rate that is second order at low pressure, where activating collisions are scarce, and first order at high pressure, where activation is fast.

The method of initial rates determines reaction orders by comparing rates measured at the very start of the reaction for systematically varied starting concentrations. Doubling [A] while holding [B] fixed and observing the rate quadruple establishes second order in A. Combining several such experiments isolates each exponent and finally yields the rate constant from the complete rate expression.

In a reaction limited by a slow first step followed by a fast step, the rate-determining step alone fixes the observed rate law. For the reaction of nitrogen dioxide with carbon monoxide, the bimolecular step 2 NO2 giving NO plus NO3 is slow, so the rate is second order in NO2 and zero order in carbon monoxide despite carbon monoxide appearing in the overall stoichiometry.

The Eyring equation expresses the rate constant as k equal to (kB T over h) times the exponential of minus the Gibbs energy of activation divided by RT. Decomposing the activation Gibbs energy into enthalpic and entropic parts gives an Eyring plot of ln(k over T) against 1 over T, whose slope yields the activation enthalpy and whose intercept yields the activation entropy.

A pseudo-first-order treatment simplifies kinetics when one reactant is held in large excess so its concentration scarcely changes. The hydrolysis of an ester in a vast excess of water follows ln[ester] decreasing linearly with time even though the true mechanism is bimolecular. The observed constant is the true second-order constant multiplied by the nearly constant water concentration.

The kinetic isotope effect arises because a carbon-deuterium bond has a lower zero-point energy than a carbon-hydrogen bond, so breaking it requires more activation energy. A primary effect with kH over kD between 6 and 8 signals that the bond to the isotopically labelled atom is broken in the rate-determining step, providing direct mechanistic evidence for the site of cleavage.

Enzyme catalysis lowers the activation barrier by stabilising the transition state more than the substrate, increasing the rate by factors that can exceed ten orders of magnitude. The catalytic proficiency, defined as the ratio kcat over Km divided by the uncatalysed rate constant, measures how tightly the enzyme binds the transition-state structure relative to the ground-state substrate.

A chain reaction proceeds through initiation, propagation, and termination steps, and may show explosive behaviour when branching steps generate more radicals than they consume. The hydrogen-oxygen reaction exhibits three explosion limits in a pressure-temperature diagram, the lower and upper limits set by competition between wall recombination, gas-phase branching, and three-body chain-terminating collisions.

A reaction approaching equilibrium has a net rate equal to the forward rate minus the reverse rate. For the reversible isomerisation A in equilibrium with B, the relaxation toward equilibrium after a perturbation is exponential with an apparent rate constant equal to the sum of the forward and reverse constants. Temperature-jump experiments exploit this to extract both microscopic constants from a single relaxation trace.

Body-centred cubic iron places one atom at each corner of the unit cell and one at the body centre, giving two atoms per cell and a packing efficiency of 68 percent. The atoms touch along the body diagonal, so the diagonal length of root three times the lattice parameter equals four atomic radii, allowing the radius to be calculated directly from the measured cell edge.

The zinc blende structure of cubic zinc sulphide has sulphide ions in a face-centred cubic array with zinc ions occupying half the tetrahedral holes in an ordered alternating pattern. Each ion is four-coordinate, and the structure is adopted by many semiconductors including gallium arsenide, whose direct band gap underpins its use in light-emitting diodes and high-frequency electronics.

Miller indices label crystal planes by the reciprocals of their fractional intercepts with the unit cell axes, cleared of fractions. The (111) plane in a cubic crystal intercepts all three axes equally, while (100) is parallel to two axes. The interplanar spacing for a cubic lattice follows 1 over d squared equal to (h squared plus k squared plus l squared) divided by the lattice parameter squared.

Polymorphism allows a single compound to crystallise in distinct lattice arrangements with different physical properties. Calcium carbonate occurs as rhombohedral calcite and orthorhombic aragonite, the former thermodynamically stable at ambient conditions. In pharmaceuticals the choice of polymorph controls dissolution rate and bioavailability, making polymorph screening a regulated step in drug development.

The radius ratio rule predicts coordination geometry in ionic solids from the ratio of cation to anion radius. A ratio between 0.414 and 0.732 favours octahedral six-coordination as in sodium chloride, while a ratio above 0.732 permits eight-coordination as in caesium chloride. The rule reflects the geometric requirement that anions not overlap while the cation contacts each of its neighbours.

Schottky defects in an ionic crystal consist of paired vacancies of cations and anions that preserve overall electroneutrality, lowering the density slightly. Frenkel defects instead displace an ion from its lattice site into an interstitial position. The equilibrium defect concentration rises exponentially with temperature according to the formation enthalpy, governing ionic conductivity in solid electrolytes.

The structure factor sums the scattering contributions of all atoms in the unit cell, each weighted by its atomic form factor and a phase determined by its fractional coordinates. Systematic absences arise when the structure factor vanishes for whole classes of reflections; a body-centred lattice extinguishes all reflections for which the sum of the indices is odd, revealing the lattice centring directly from the diffraction pattern.

Hexagonal close packing stacks layers in an ABAB sequence, while cubic close packing follows ABCABC. Both achieve the maximum packing efficiency of 74 percent with twelve nearest neighbours, but they differ in the number and arrangement of tetrahedral and octahedral holes available for interstitial atoms, which is why magnesium adopts one and copper the other despite similar atomic sizes.

The perovskite structure with general formula ABO3 places a large A cation at the cube corners, a smaller B cation at the body centre, and oxide ions at the face centres. The Goldschmidt tolerance factor, computed from the three ionic radii, predicts whether the ideal cubic structure is stable or distorts to tetragonal or orthorhombic symmetry, which underlies the ferroelectric behaviour of barium titanate.

Twinning occurs when two crystal domains share a lattice plane related by a symmetry operation not present in the single crystal, such as a mirror or rotation. Merohedral twinning, in which the twin lattice coincides exactly with the crystal lattice, can mimic higher symmetry and corrupt structure determination unless detected through statistical analysis of reflection intensities.

A stereocentre bearing four different substituents is assigned R or S by ranking the substituents by Cahn-Ingold-Prelog priority and viewing the molecule with the lowest priority group pointing away. A clockwise descent through the remaining three from highest to lowest priority denotes R, counterclockwise denotes S. The descriptor is independent of the sign of optical rotation.

Diastereomers differ in configuration at one or more but not all stereocentres and therefore have distinct physical properties, unlike enantiomers which are identical except in chiral environments. Tartaric acid has three stereoisomers: a pair of enantiomers and an achiral meso form whose internal mirror plane makes its two stereocentres cancel, so it is optically inactive despite containing stereocentres.

Atropisomerism is a form of chirality arising from restricted rotation about a single bond rather than from a stereocentre. In biphenyls bearing bulky ortho substituents the two rings cannot become coplanar, freezing the molecule into a twisted shape that exists as separable enantiomeric conformers. The barrier to interconversion must exceed about 90 kilojoules per mole for the atropisomers to be isolable at room temperature.

A racemic mixture contains equal amounts of two enantiomers and shows no net optical rotation. Resolution separates the enantiomers, classically by converting them with an enantiopure resolving agent into diastereomeric salts that differ in solubility and can be crystallised apart. After separation the resolving agent is removed by acid or base, recovering each enantiomer in pure form.

The optical rotation observed in a polarimeter depends on concentration, path length, wavelength, temperature, and solvent. The specific rotation normalises these factors as the observed rotation divided by the product of concentration in grams per millilitre and path length in decimetres. Sucrose has a specific rotation of plus 66.5 degrees at the sodium D line, and its hydrolysis to glucose and fructose inverts the sign, the origin of the term invert sugar.

Prochirality describes a centre that becomes a stereocentre upon a single substitution. The two hydrogens on the methylene carbon of ethanol are enantiotopic, indistinguishable in an achiral environment but distinguished by an enzyme. Alcohol dehydrogenase removes specifically the pro-R hydrogen, demonstrating that biological catalysts can select between groups that are equivalent to ordinary reagents.

Allenes possess axial chirality when each terminal carbon bears two different substituents, because the two pi systems are mutually perpendicular and place the four groups in a non-planar arrangement. The molecule and its mirror image are non-superimposable even though no atom is a classical stereocentre, so the descriptors aR and aS or M and P are used to specify the configuration along the axis.

Conformational analysis of cyclohexane shows the chair as the lowest-energy form, with substituents preferring equatorial positions to avoid 1,3-diaxial strain. The A value quantifies this preference; tert-butyl has an A value near 21 kilojoules per mole, so it locks the ring with the bulky group equatorial. Ring flipping interconverts axial and equatorial positions through the higher-energy twist-boat.

Asymmetric synthesis builds a new stereocentre with preference for one configuration, measured by enantiomeric excess. Sharpless epoxidation of allylic alcohols with titanium isopropoxide, a tartrate ester, and tert-butyl hydroperoxide delivers epoxides with excess routinely above 90 percent, the chiral tartrate controlling which face of the alkene is oxidised.

An SN2 reaction proceeds with inversion of configuration because the nucleophile attacks the carbon from the side opposite the leaving group, passing through a trigonal bipyramidal transition state. When the carbon is a stereocentre, this Walden inversion converts an R substrate cleanly into an S product, providing a stereochemical fingerprint that distinguishes the concerted bimolecular mechanism from a racemising SN1 pathway.

The integration of a proton NMR signal is proportional to the number of equivalent protons giving rise to it. In ethyl acetate the spectrum shows a triplet near 1.2 ppm integrating for three, a singlet near 2.0 ppm integrating for three, and a quartet near 4.1 ppm integrating for two, the relative areas immediately revealing the ethyl and acetyl fragments.

The n plus one rule predicts that a proton coupled to n equivalent neighbours appears as a multiplet of n plus one lines with intensities given by Pascal's triangle. An isopropyl group shows a doublet for the six methyl protons split by the single methine proton, and a septet for that methine split by the six methyls, a pattern that diagnoses the fragment at a glance.

Carbon-13 NMR exploits the 1.1 percent natural abundance of the carbon-13 nucleus to count distinct carbon environments. Proton decoupling collapses the carbon-proton multiplets to singlets, simplifying the spectrum, while a DEPT-135 experiment encodes the number of attached hydrogens, displaying methyl and methine carbons positive and methylene carbons negative, with quaternary carbons absent.

The chemical shift of a proton reflects the local electron density that shields it from the applied field. Protons near electronegative atoms or in the deshielding cone of an aromatic ring resonate downfield; aromatic protons appear near 7 ppm and aldehyde protons near 10 ppm, while shielded protons on saturated carbons cluster between 0.5 and 2 ppm.

Two-dimensional COSY correlates protons that share a scalar coupling, placing cross-peaks off the diagonal wherever two signals are spin-coupled. Tracing a chain of cross-peaks walks the analyst along a connected sequence of carbon-bound protons, mapping the carbon skeleton fragment by fragment without prior assumptions about the structure.

The nuclear Overhauser effect transfers magnetisation between nuclei close in space through dipolar relaxation, its intensity falling off as the inverse sixth power of internuclear distance. A NOESY spectrum therefore reveals which protons lie within about five angstroms of each other, distinguishing cis from trans alkene geometry and establishing the three-dimensional fold of a peptide.

Coupling constants carry geometric information through the Karplus relationship, which expresses the three-bond proton-proton coupling as a function of the dihedral angle. Couplings near 8 to 12 hertz indicate dihedral angles close to 0 or 180 degrees, while couplings near 2 to 4 hertz correspond to angles near 90 degrees, allowing ring conformations to be deduced from the spectrum.

An HSQC experiment correlates each proton with the carbon to which it is directly bonded, producing a single cross-peak per carbon-hydrogen pair. Overlapping proton signals that defy assignment in one dimension separate cleanly when spread against the wider carbon dispersion, making HSQC indispensable for unravelling crowded spectra of complex natural products.

Exchangeable protons on heteroatoms such as hydroxyl and amine groups often appear as broad signals at variable chemical shift because rapid proton exchange averages the environment. Adding a drop of deuterium oxide replaces these protons with deuterium, causing the corresponding signals to vanish, a simple test that identifies which peaks belong to exchangeable hydrogens.

Long-range correlations in an HMBC experiment connect protons to carbons two and three bonds away, bridging the gaps left by directly bonded HSQC correlations. A proton showing an HMBC cross-peak to a carbonyl carbon establishes that the proton sits alpha or beta to that carbonyl, knitting together fragments across quaternary carbons and heteroatoms that interrupt the proton-coupled network.

The dioxygen molecule is paramagnetic because its molecular orbital configuration places two electrons singly in the degenerate pi-antibonding orbitals. Filling the orbitals in order of energy gives a bond order of two, consistent with the observed bond strength, while the two unpaired electrons explain why liquid oxygen is attracted to a magnet, a fact that valence bond theory fails to predict.

The bond order of a diatomic molecule equals half the difference between the number of electrons in bonding and antibonding orbitals. The dinitrogen molecule has a bond order of three from its filled sigma and pi bonding orbitals with empty antibonding orbitals, accounting for its short bond and exceptional kinetic inertness toward most reagents at ordinary temperature.

For second-row diatomics lighter than oxygen, the 2s and 2p sigma orbitals lie close enough in energy to mix, raising the sigma-2p orbital above the pi-2p pair. This s-p mixing reorders the molecular orbital diagram so that boron and carbon diatomics fill the pi orbitals before the sigma, explaining why B2 is paramagnetic with two unpaired electrons.

Benzene's pi system is treated by combining six parallel p orbitals into six delocalised molecular orbitals. Three are bonding and fully occupied by the six pi electrons, satisfying the Huckel count of 4n plus 2 for aromatic stability. The lowest orbital has no nodes, and the degenerate pair above it each carry one node, producing the exceptional thermodynamic stability of the aromatic ring.

Frontier molecular orbital theory focuses on the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals to predict reactivity. A nucleophile donates electron density from its HOMO into the LUMO of an electrophile, and the strongest interaction occurs when the two orbitals are close in energy and overlap well, rationalising the regioselectivity of additions and the rates of cycloadditions.

The hydrogen molecular ion, with one electron and two protons, is the simplest system whose Schrodinger equation can be solved to illustrate molecular orbital formation. The symmetric combination of the two atomic 1s functions concentrates electron density between the nuclei and is bonding, while the antisymmetric combination has a node between the nuclei and is antibonding, raising the energy.

Walsh diagrams plot orbital energies against a geometric parameter such as bond angle, predicting the preferred shape of a molecule. For an AH2 species the diagram shows that filling the orbital that stabilises a bent geometry drives water to its 104.5 degree angle, whereas beryllium hydride, with fewer electrons, remains linear because no electron occupies the angle-sensitive orbital.

Carbon monoxide has a small dipole moment with the negative end surprisingly on carbon, despite oxygen being more electronegative. Molecular orbital theory resolves the paradox: the highest occupied orbital is largely a carbon lone pair pointing away from oxygen, and this orbital, donated to metals in carbonyl complexes, makes carbon monoxide a strong sigma donor through its carbon end.

The allyl system of three p orbitals yields three pi molecular orbitals: a bonding orbital with no node, a non-bonding orbital with a node on the central carbon, and an antibonding orbital with two nodes. The allyl cation, radical, and anion differ only in the occupancy of the non-bonding orbital, which is why all three species share the same delocalised charge distribution over the terminal carbons.

Conjugation lowers the energy gap between the highest occupied and lowest unoccupied orbitals as the pi system lengthens. In a series of polyenes the absorption maximum shifts to longer wavelength with each added double bond, so beta-carotene with eleven conjugated double bonds absorbs in the blue-green and appears orange, a direct visible consequence of molecular orbital spacing.

Permanganate is a powerful oxidant whose half-reaction in acid, the manganese centre going from plus seven to plus two, consumes five electrons and eight protons per ion and is accompanied by the disappearance of the intense purple colour. In neutral or basic solution the reduction stops at brown manganese dioxide, a three-electron change that leaves the manganese in the plus four state.

The dichromate ion in acidic solution is reduced to chromium in the plus three oxidation state, gaining six electrons per dichromate and turning from orange to green. This colour change underlies the classical breathalyser test, in which ethanol reduces dichromate, and the extent of the colour shift quantifies the amount of alcohol oxidised to acetic acid.

A Latimer diagram strings together standard reduction potentials connecting the oxidation states of an element. Comparing adjacent potentials reveals disproportionation: copper in the plus one state is unstable in water because the potential for its reduction to the metal exceeds that for its oxidation to the plus two state, so it spontaneously splits into copper metal and the cupric ion.

Inner-sphere electron transfer proceeds through a bridging ligand shared between the oxidant and reductant, as Taube demonstrated when chloride transferred from a cobalt complex to chromium during the redox event. Outer-sphere transfer instead occurs without bond breaking, the electron tunnelling between intact coordination spheres, with rates described by Marcus theory in terms of reorganisation energy.

The Fenton reaction generates hydroxyl radicals when ferrous iron reduces hydrogen peroxide, the iron being oxidised to the ferric state. The highly reactive radical attacks organic substrates indiscriminately. Cycling the iron back to the plus two state with a co-reductant sustains the catalysis, the basis of advanced oxidation processes for destroying recalcitrant pollutants in wastewater.

Standard reduction potentials predict whether a metal will displace another from solution. Zinc, with a potential of minus 0.76 volts, reduces copper ions because copper sits higher in the electrochemical series at plus 0.34 volts. Dropping a zinc strip into copper sulphate deposits copper metal and dissolves zinc, the cell potential of 1.10 volts confirming the spontaneity of the displacement.

Cerium in the plus four state is a clean one-electron oxidant widely used in titrimetry because its reduction to the plus three state involves no change in coordination geometry and no oxygen transfer. The sharp potential near 1.44 volts in sulphuric acid and the stability of the reagent make ceric titrations a precise alternative to permanganate for determining iron and oxalate.

The Nernst equation corrects a standard potential for non-standard concentrations, the potential decreasing by 59 millivolts per decade increase in the ratio of oxidised to reduced species for a one-electron couple. For the ferric-ferrous couple this means the measured potential reports directly on the activity ratio, allowing redox titrations to be followed potentiometrically to a precise endpoint.

Vanadium displays a vivid sequence of oxidation states distinguishable by colour: the yellow dioxovanadium plus five ion, the blue oxovanadium plus four ion, the green plus three ion, and the violet plus two ion. Reducing an acidified vanadate solution with zinc amalgam steps the metal down through all four states, each transition marked by a clean colour change visible to the eye.

A Frost diagram plots the product of oxidation state and standard potential against oxidation state, so the slope between two points gives the potential of the corresponding couple. A species lying above the line joining its neighbours is thermodynamically poised to disproportionate, while one lying below is the stable product of comproportionation, making the diagram a compact map of redox stability.

The Woodward-Hoffmann rules govern pericyclic reactions through conservation of orbital symmetry. For thermal electrocyclic ring closures, a system with 4n pi electrons closes conrotatory while a system with 4n plus 2 closes disrotatory. Photochemical excitation reverses these preferences, because promoting an electron changes the symmetry of the highest occupied orbital that controls the rotation.

The Cope rearrangement is a degenerate [3,3]-sigmatropic shift of 1,5-hexadiene in which a sigma bond migrates across the ends of two allyl fragments through a six-membered chair-like transition state. The reaction interconverts identical structures, so it is detected only by isotopic labelling, which shows the labelled carbons exchanging positions as the bond reorganises.

The Claisen rearrangement of an allyl vinyl ether is a [3,3]-sigmatropic process that converts the ether into a gamma,delta-unsaturated carbonyl compound. The reaction is exothermic because a weaker carbon-oxygen pi bond is traded for a stronger carbon-oxygen sigma bond, and it proceeds through an ordered chair-like transition state that transfers chirality with high fidelity.

A 1,3-dipolar cycloaddition combines a 1,3-dipole such as an azide with a dipolarophile such as an alkyne to form a five-membered ring. The reaction is a [3+2] process under orbital-symmetry control, and the copper-catalysed version of the azide-alkyne coupling delivers 1,4-disubstituted triazoles regioselectively, the cornerstone reaction of click chemistry.

A sigmatropic hydrogen shift relocates a hydrogen atom along a pi system together with the sigma bond that holds it. A thermal [1,5] hydrogen shift in a cyclopentadiene is suprafacial and symmetry allowed, the hydrogen moving across the same face of the ring, whereas a thermal [1,3] shift would require an antarafacial geometry that is too strained to occur readily.

The cheletropic extrusion of sulphur dioxide from a cyclic sulphone expels the small molecule in a single concerted step, leaving behind a diene. The reverse addition of sulphur dioxide to a diene is likewise concerted, and the linear or non-linear approach of the extruding fragment is dictated by orbital symmetry, in parallel with the rules governing electrocyclic reactions.

An ene reaction couples an alkene bearing an allylic hydrogen, the ene component, with an electron-poor enophile. In a single concerted step the allylic hydrogen transfers to the enophile, a new sigma bond forms between the terminal carbons, and the double bond migrates within the ene component. The reaction proceeds through a six-electron transition state resembling that of a retro-Diels-Alder.

The retro-Diels-Alder reaction fragments a cyclohexene into a diene and a dienophile when entropy and the release of a stable small molecule favour it. Cyclopentadiene stored as its dimer cracks on heating, the dimer undergoing retro-Diels-Alder to regenerate two molecules of monomer that are collected by distillation before they redimerise.

The thermal ring opening of cyclobutene to butadiene is an electrocyclic reaction of a four-electron system and therefore proceeds conrotatory. When the cyclobutene bears two methyl groups, the conrotatory motion dictates which geometric isomer of the diene forms; the cis dimethyl compound opens exclusively to one stereoisomer, a clean experimental test of the orbital-symmetry prediction.

The aromatic transition state model rationalises pericyclic selectivity by counting electrons in the cyclic array of interacting orbitals. A transition state with 4n plus 2 electrons and zero phase inversions is Huckel aromatic and thermally allowed, while one with the same electron count and an odd number of inversions is Mobius and requires photochemical activation, reproducing the Woodward-Hoffmann conclusions.

Glucose exists in solution as an equilibrium mixture of cyclic hemiacetal forms. The open-chain aldehyde closes when the C5 hydroxyl attacks the carbonyl, creating a new stereocentre at C1 called the anomeric carbon. The alpha and beta anomers, differing only in the orientation of the anomeric hydroxyl, interconvert through the open chain in the process of mutarotation.

Mutarotation of glucose is observed as a change in optical rotation when freshly dissolved crystals reach equilibrium. Pure alpha-glucose starts at plus 112 degrees and pure beta-glucose at plus 19 degrees, and both drift to the equilibrium value of plus 52.7 degrees, corresponding to a mixture of roughly 36 percent alpha and 64 percent beta, with a trace of the open-chain form.

A glycosidic bond forms when the anomeric hydroxyl of one sugar condenses with a hydroxyl of another, eliminating water. In maltose two glucose units are joined by an alpha-1,4 linkage, whereas in cellobiose the same units are joined by a beta-1,4 linkage. The difference in anomeric configuration is why starch is digestible by human enzymes while cellulose is not.

Reducing sugars possess a free anomeric carbon that can open to an aldehyde and reduce Tollens or Fehling reagents. Glucose and maltose are reducing, but sucrose is not, because its glycosidic bond joins the anomeric carbons of both glucose and fructose, locking each ring closed so neither can open to expose a reactive carbonyl.

Epimers are sugars that differ in configuration at a single stereocentre. Glucose and galactose are C4 epimers, while glucose and mannose are C2 epimers. The Lobry de Bruyn-Alberda van Ekenstein rearrangement interconverts glucose, mannose, and fructose under mild base through a common enediol intermediate, scrambling the configuration at C2 and shifting the carbonyl between C1 and C2.

The Fischer projection draws a sugar with the carbon chain vertical and the carbonyl at the top. Horizontal bonds point toward the viewer and vertical bonds away. A D sugar has the hydroxyl on the highest-numbered stereocentre pointing right, and the assignment is made by reference to D-glyceraldehyde, the configurational standard from which the entire sugar family is derived.

Pyranose rings adopt chair conformations, and beta-D-glucopyranose is exceptionally stable because every bulky substituent, including all four hydroxyls and the hydroxymethyl group, can occupy an equatorial position simultaneously. This all-equatorial arrangement minimises 1,3-diaxial strain and accounts for glucose being the most abundant monosaccharide in nature.

Osazone formation occurs when a reducing sugar reacts with three equivalents of phenylhydrazine, derivatising both C1 and C2 as phenylhydrazones. Because C2 is consumed, glucose, mannose, and fructose all yield the identical osazone, a classic observation that established their stereochemical relationship at C3, C4, and C5 long before modern spectroscopy.

The anomeric effect describes the preference of an electronegative substituent at the anomeric carbon for the axial rather than the equatorial position, against ordinary steric expectation. The effect is attributed to favourable donation from a ring-oxygen lone pair into the antibonding orbital of the axial carbon-substituent bond, and it strongly influences the conformations of glycosides.

Amylose and amylopectin are the two polymers of starch, both built from alpha-glucose. Amylose is a linear alpha-1,4 chain that coils into a helix and gives the deep blue complex with iodine, while amylopectin carries alpha-1,6 branch points every twenty-odd residues, producing a bushy structure that is rapidly mobilised by enzymes attacking many chain ends at once.

The diagonal relationship pairs an element with the one to its lower right, which often shares similar charge density. Lithium resembles magnesium more than the other alkali metals: both form covalent organometallics, burn in nitrogen to give nitrides, and have sparingly soluble carbonates and fluorides, a similarity traced to comparable ionic radius to charge ratios.

The inert pair effect explains why the heavier p-block elements favour an oxidation state two below the group maximum. Lead is far more stable as plus two than plus four, and bismuth as plus three rather than plus five, because the 6s electrons are poorly shielded, contracted by relativistic effects, and reluctant to participate in bonding.

Allotropy in the p-block is dramatic for phosphorus. White phosphorus consists of strained tetrahedral P4 molecules, highly reactive and spontaneously flammable in air, while red phosphorus is an amorphous polymeric network that is far less reactive. Black phosphorus, the thermodynamically stable form, is a layered semiconductor structurally analogous to graphite.

Silicon and carbon differ sharply despite sharing group 14. Carbon forms strong pi bonds and exists as carbon dioxide, a discrete molecule with carbon-oxygen double bonds, whereas silicon forms weak pi bonds and instead builds silicon dioxide as an extended covalent network of corner-sharing tetrahedra, which is why quartz is a hard high-melting solid and carbon dioxide a gas.

The halogens grade smoothly in physical state from gaseous fluorine and chlorine through liquid bromine to solid iodine as dispersion forces strengthen with increasing electron count. Their oxidising power falls down the group, so chlorine displaces bromide and iodide from solution while iodine cannot displace the lighter halides, a reactivity order confirmed by standard electrode potentials.

Boron is electron deficient and forms a remarkable family of cluster hydrides. Diborane has no ordinary two-centre bonds between its borons; instead two bridging hydrogens each form a three-centre two-electron bond spanning two boron atoms and one hydrogen, a bonding motif that resolves the apparent shortage of valence electrons in the molecule.

The noble gases were long thought wholly unreactive until xenon was found to combine with the most powerful oxidants. Xenon difluoride, tetrafluoride, and hexafluoride form by direct reaction with fluorine, the heavier noble gas being oxidisable because its outermost electrons are weakly held. Xenon trioxide is a dangerously explosive solid that hydrolyses from the hexafluoride.

Sulphur catenates more readily than oxygen, forming chains and rings because the sulphur-sulphur single bond is comparatively strong. The thermodynamically stable form at room temperature is the crown-shaped S8 ring, which on melting and further heating opens into long polymeric chains, sharply increasing the viscosity of the liquid before it falls again near the boiling point.

Aluminium chloride exists as the dimer Al2Cl6 in the vapour and in non-coordinating solvents, each aluminium completing an octet by accepting a chloride lone pair from its partner through a bridging bond. The dimer dissociates to the monomeric trigonal planar molecule at high temperature, and in the monomer the electron-deficient aluminium is a potent Lewis acid catalyst.

Across a period the oxides change from basic through amphoteric to acidic as the elements become more electronegative. Sodium oxide dissolves in water to give a strong alkali, aluminium oxide reacts with both acids and bases, and sulphur trioxide dissolves to give sulphuric acid, the trend mirroring the shift from ionic metal oxides to covalent non-metal oxides.

The ideal gas law PV equals nRT combines the empirical relations of Boyle, Charles, and Avogadro into a single equation of state. For one mole of gas at 273.15 kelvin and one atmosphere the molar volume works out to 22.4 litres, a benchmark that follows directly from substituting the gas constant 8.314 joules per mole kelvin and converting units consistently.

Real gases deviate from ideality at high pressure and low temperature, and the van der Waals equation corrects for this with two terms. The a constant accounts for attractive intermolecular forces that reduce the measured pressure, and the b constant subtracts the finite volume occupied by the molecules themselves, giving (P plus a n squared over V squared) times (V minus n b) equal to nRT.

Graham's law states that the rate of effusion of a gas is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass. Hydrogen effuses four times faster than oxygen because the mass ratio is sixteen and its square root is four. The principle was exploited in the gaseous diffusion enrichment of uranium hexafluoride, where the isotopic mass difference is tiny.

The kinetic theory of gases derives pressure from molecular collisions with the container walls, yielding the result that pressure times volume equals one third of N m times the mean square speed. Equating this to nRT shows that the average translational kinetic energy of a molecule is three halves kT, depending only on temperature and not on the identity of the gas.

The Maxwell-Boltzmann speed distribution describes the spread of molecular speeds in a gas at thermal equilibrium. The curve rises from zero, peaks at the most probable speed, and tails off at high speed. Raising the temperature broadens and flattens the distribution and shifts the peak to higher speed, increasing the fraction of molecules energetic enough to surmount a reaction barrier.

Dalton's law of partial pressures states that the total pressure of a gas mixture equals the sum of the pressures each component would exert alone. When a gas is collected over water the measured pressure includes the water vapour pressure, which must be subtracted before applying the ideal gas law to find the moles of the dry gas collected.

The compressibility factor Z, defined as PV divided by nRT, equals one for an ideal gas and measures the departure of a real gas from ideality. At moderate pressures Z dips below one as attractive forces dominate, then rises above one at very high pressure when the finite molecular volume makes the gas harder to compress than the ideal model predicts.

The root mean square speed of gas molecules equals the square root of three RT divided by the molar mass. For nitrogen at room temperature this gives roughly 515 metres per second, close to the speed of sound in air, while a heavier gas such as carbon dioxide moves more slowly under identical conditions because its larger molar mass appears in the denominator.

The mean free path is the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, equal to kT divided by the product of root two, pressure, and collision cross-section. At atmospheric pressure it is about 70 nanometres for air, but in a high vacuum it lengthens to metres, which is why molecular beam experiments and thin-film deposition demand low pressures.

The Joule-Thomson effect describes the temperature change of a real gas forced through a throttle at constant enthalpy. Below its inversion temperature a gas cools on expansion because work is done against attractive forces, the basis of gas liquefaction. Hydrogen and helium have inversion temperatures below room temperature, so they warm on throttling unless precooled first.

An iodometric titration determines an oxidising analyte indirectly by letting it liberate iodine from excess iodide, then titrating the liberated iodine with standard thiosulphate. The endpoint is sharpened by adding starch near the equivalence point, which forms a deep blue complex with iodine that vanishes abruptly when the last of the iodine is reduced to iodide.

Standardising a potassium permanganate solution against primary-standard sodium oxalate exploits the self-indicating nature of permanganate. Oxalate is oxidised to carbon dioxide while manganese drops from plus seven to plus two, and the titration is run warm and acidic. The endpoint is the first persistent faint pink, signalling a trace excess of unreduced permanganate.

The Winkler method measures dissolved oxygen by fixing it as a manganese precipitate, which oxidises iodide to iodine on acidification. Titrating the iodine with thiosulphate quantifies the original oxygen, since each mole of oxygen ultimately accounts for four moles of thiosulphate. The technique remains a reference standard for assessing the oxygen content of natural waters.

In a redox titration the potential of the solution is governed by the couple in excess, jumping sharply at the equivalence point as control passes from the analyte couple to the titrant couple. The equivalence-point potential is a weighted average of the two standard potentials, the weights set by the number of electrons each half-reaction transfers.

A redox indicator changes colour over a narrow potential range bracketing its own standard potential, by analogy with the way a pH indicator responds to a span of pH. Ferroin, the iron complex of phenanthroline, switches from pale blue to red near 1.06 volts and is the indicator of choice for titrations with cerium and dichromate.

Determining the iron content of an ore by dichromate titration requires the iron first to be fully reduced to the ferrous state, often with stannous chloride, with the slight excess of reductant destroyed by mercuric chloride. The ferrous iron is then titrated with standard dichromate, and the volume at the endpoint yields the percentage of iron by simple stoichiometry.

The chemical oxygen demand of a water sample is measured by refluxing it with excess dichromate in strong sulphuric acid with a silver catalyst. Organic matter is oxidised, consuming dichromate in proportion to its concentration, and the unreacted dichromate is back-titrated with ferrous ammonium sulphate, the difference revealing how much oxidant the pollutants consumed.

A back-titration suits a slow or insoluble analyte. To assay calcium carbonate the sample is dissolved in a measured excess of standard hydrochloric acid, and after reaction is complete the unconsumed acid is titrated with standard sodium hydroxide. Subtracting the base used from the acid originally added gives the acid that the carbonate consumed.

Karl Fischer titration determines trace water through the reaction of iodine, sulphur dioxide, a base, and an alcohol, in which water is consumed stoichiometrically with iodine. In the coulometric variant the iodine is generated electrochemically, and the charge passed measures the iodine produced, allowing water contents down to a few parts per million to be quantified precisely.

The titration of hydrogen peroxide with permanganate proceeds in acidic solution with peroxide acting as the reductant, oxygen gas being evolved as the peroxide oxygen goes from minus one to zero. Two moles of permanganate react with five moles of peroxide, and the persistence of a pale pink tinge marks the equivalence point without a separate indicator.

Hydrogen bonding occurs when a hydrogen atom bonded to a small electronegative atom is attracted to a lone pair on another such atom. The anomalously high boiling point of water, far above that of hydrogen sulphide, arises because each water molecule forms up to four hydrogen bonds, a three-dimensional network that must be partly broken before the liquid can vaporise.

London dispersion forces arise from instantaneous fluctuations in electron density that create transient dipoles inducing dipoles in neighbours. Their strength grows with molecular polarisability, which is why the boiling points of the noble gases rise steadily from helium to xenon and why larger hydrocarbons are liquids and waxes while methane is a gas.

Dipole-dipole attractions act between polar molecules whose permanent dipoles align so that opposite partial charges face each other. Acetone, with its polar carbonyl, boils considerably higher than the non-polar hydrocarbon of similar mass, the difference measuring the extra energy needed to overcome dipolar alignment in addition to dispersion forces.

The boiling point trend across the hydrides of group 15, 16, and 17 shows ammonia, water, and hydrogen fluoride lying anomalously high above their heavier congeners. The deviation is the signature of hydrogen bonding; without it, extrapolation of the dispersion-force trend would predict water to boil near minus 80 degrees Celsius and leave Earth without liquid oceans.

Ion-dipole forces stabilise ions dissolved in a polar solvent, the partial charges of the solvent orienting toward the ion of opposite sign. The hydration of sodium and chloride ions by surrounding water shells releases enough enthalpy to compensate the lattice energy of sodium chloride, which is why an ionic solid held together by strong electrostatic forces nonetheless dissolves readily in water.

Surface tension arises because molecules at a liquid surface experience a net inward attraction, having fewer neighbours than those in the bulk. Water has a high surface tension of about 72 millinewtons per metre at room temperature, a direct consequence of its hydrogen-bonding network, which allows small insects to stand on a pond and droplets to bead on a waxy leaf.

Intramolecular hydrogen bonding can override the intermolecular variety. Ortho-nitrophenol forms an internal hydrogen bond between its hydroxyl and nitro groups, so it has little capacity left to bond with neighbours and is steam-volatile, whereas para-nitrophenol bonds extensively between molecules, raising its melting point and lowering its volatility markedly.

The polarity of a solvent, expressed through its dielectric constant, governs what it dissolves. Water with a dielectric constant near 80 screens ionic charges effectively and dissolves salts, while hexane with a dielectric constant near 2 dissolves only non-polar substances, the empirical rule that like dissolves like resting on the matching of intermolecular force types.

The hydrophobic effect drives non-polar molecules together in water, not because they attract one another strongly but because clustering minimises the disruption of the hydrogen-bonded solvent. Ordered cage-like water around an isolated non-polar solute is entropically costly, so the system reduces the exposed non-polar surface, an effect central to micelle formation and protein folding.

Van der Waals radii define the effective size of an atom in non-bonded contact, the distance of closest approach before repulsion dominates. The van der Waals radius of hydrogen is about 120 picometres, and steric strain in crowded molecules arises when atoms are forced closer than the sum of their van der Waals radii, raising the energy through repulsive overlap.

A primary alcohol is oxidised to an aldehyde and then further to a carboxylic acid by chromium-based reagents in aqueous acid. To stop cleanly at the aldehyde, a milder anhydrous oxidant such as pyridinium chlorochromate is used, since it lacks the water needed to form the hydrate that the chromium would otherwise oxidise onward to the acid.

Reduction of a carboxylic acid to a primary alcohol requires a powerful hydride donor such as lithium aluminium hydride, since the carboxyl group is resistant to milder reagents. Sodium borohydride, by contrast, reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but leaves carboxylic acids and esters untouched, a selectivity exploited when only one carbonyl in a molecule is to be reduced.

A nitrile is hydrolysed to a carboxylic acid under either acidic or basic aqueous conditions, passing through an amide intermediate. The transformation extends a carbon chain by one carbon when the nitrile is first installed by displacing a halide with cyanide, providing a classic two-step route from an alkyl halide to the homologous carboxylic acid.

An ester is cleaved to a carboxylate salt and an alcohol by aqueous base in the reaction known as saponification. The mechanism proceeds through a tetrahedral intermediate formed by hydroxide addition to the carbonyl, and because the carboxylate product is stabilised and unreactive toward the alcohol, the reaction is irreversible, unlike acid-catalysed ester hydrolysis.

A ketone reacts with a primary amine to form an imine, eliminating water through a carbinolamine intermediate. The equilibrium is driven toward the imine by removing water, often with a desiccant or by azeotropic distillation. Reductive amination short-circuits the isolation by reducing the imine in situ with sodium cyanoborohydride to give a secondary amine.

An alkene is cleaved oxidatively by ozone, the resulting ozonide being worked up reductively with dimethyl sulphide to give two carbonyl compounds. Each doubly bonded carbon becomes a carbonyl carbon, so the structure of an unknown alkene can be deduced by identifying the fragments, an analytical use that complements ozonolysis as a synthetic step.

A carboxylic acid is converted to a more reactive acid chloride by thionyl chloride, which expels sulphur dioxide and hydrogen chloride as gases that escape the flask and drive the reaction forward. The acid chloride then acylates alcohols and amines readily, serving as the activated intermediate in the preparation of esters and amides that the acid itself forms only sluggishly.

A primary amide is dehydrated to a nitrile by a strong dehydrating agent such as phosphorus pentoxide or thionyl chloride. The two oxygens and one of the nitrogen hydrogens are removed as water and the carbon-nitrogen bond order rises to three. The reverse partial hydration, nitrile to amide, can be arranged to stop at the amide under carefully controlled conditions.

A halogen on a benzene ring resists ordinary nucleophilic substitution, but a diazonium salt made from an aromatic amine is a versatile precursor. Treatment with cuprous halides in the Sandmeyer reaction installs chloride or bromide, with cuprous cyanide installs a nitrile, and with hot water installs a phenol, all by displacement of nitrogen gas.

An epoxide is opened by nucleophiles under both acidic and basic conditions, but with opposite regioselectivity. Under basic conditions the nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon in an SN2 fashion, whereas under acidic conditions the protonated epoxide develops carbocation character at the more substituted carbon, directing the nucleophile there instead.

The carbon of methane is sp3 hybridised, four equivalent orbitals formed by mixing one 2s and three 2p orbitals pointing to the corners of a tetrahedron at 109.5 degrees. Each overlaps with a hydrogen 1s orbital to give four identical sigma bonds, explaining why all four carbon-hydrogen bonds in methane are of equal length and strength.

In ethene each carbon is sp2 hybridised, with three trigonal-planar sigma bonds and one unhybridised p orbital. The two p orbitals overlap sideways to form the pi bond, which lies above and below the molecular plane. Rotation about the double bond would break this pi overlap, accounting for the high barrier that locks alkene geometry into cis or trans.

VSEPR theory predicts molecular shape by arranging electron domains around a central atom to minimise repulsion. Ammonia has four domains, three bonding and one lone pair, giving a tetrahedral electron arrangement but a trigonal pyramidal molecular shape. The lone pair repels more strongly than bonding pairs, compressing the bond angle to 107 degrees below the ideal tetrahedral value.

The triple bond of ethyne involves sp hybridised carbons whose two sp orbitals lie 180 degrees apart, making the molecule linear. The remaining two p orbitals on each carbon form two mutually perpendicular pi bonds. The high s character of the sp orbitals draws bonding electrons closer to carbon, making the carbon-hydrogen bond acidic enough to be deprotonated by strong base.

Formal charge is assigned by giving each atom its non-bonding electrons plus half the bonding electrons, then subtracting from the free-atom valence count. Among resonance structures the one with formal charges closest to zero, and any negative charge on the most electronegative atom, is the largest contributor to the resonance hybrid.

Resonance delocalises electrons over several positions when a single Lewis structure cannot represent the bonding. The carbonate ion is drawn with one double and two single carbon-oxygen bonds, but the true structure is the average of three equivalent resonance forms, so all three bonds are identical with a length and strength intermediate between single and double.

Bond polarity is set by the electronegativity difference between bonded atoms. A difference above roughly 1.7 gives a predominantly ionic bond, an intermediate difference gives a polar covalent bond, and a small or zero difference gives a non-polar covalent bond. The vector sum of bond dipoles and lone-pair contributions yields the overall molecular dipole moment.

Expanded octets appear in third-row and heavier elements, which can accommodate more than eight valence electrons. Sulphur in sulphur hexafluoride is surrounded by six bonding pairs in an octahedral arrangement. Modern bonding descriptions favour three-centre four-electron interactions over genuine d-orbital participation to account for the hypervalent geometry.

Bond enthalpy measures the energy needed to break a bond homolytically in the gas phase, averaged over many molecules. Estimating a reaction enthalpy by summing the bonds broken and subtracting the bonds formed gives a useful approximation, accurate to within tens of kilojoules because real bond strengths vary somewhat with their molecular environment.

The carbon dioxide molecule is linear and non-polar despite containing two polar carbon-oxygen bonds, because the bond dipoles point in opposite directions and cancel. Water, by contrast, is bent, so its two oxygen-hydrogen bond dipoles add to a net dipole moment, the geometric difference accounting for the contrasting physical properties of the two simple oxides.

The solubility product of silver chloride is 1.8e-10 at 25 degrees Celsius, so in pure water the molar solubility is the square root of that value, about 1.3e-5 moles per litre. Both ion concentrations equal this figure, and any combination of silver and chloride concentrations whose product exceeds the solubility product will precipitate solid silver chloride.

The common ion effect suppresses solubility when one of the ions of a sparingly soluble salt is already present. Silver chloride is far less soluble in dilute sodium chloride than in pure water, because the elevated chloride concentration forces the equilibrium back toward the solid in accordance with the fixed value of the solubility product.

Selective precipitation separates ions that form salts of differing solubility. Adding chloride slowly to a solution of silver and lead ions first precipitates silver chloride, the less soluble salt, and only when its ion product is satisfied does lead chloride begin to form. The gap in solubility products defines how cleanly the two metals can be separated.

The solubility of many metal sulphides is strongly pH dependent because sulphide is the conjugate base of a weak acid. In acidic solution the low sulphide concentration keeps zinc sulphide dissolved while the far less soluble copper sulphide still precipitates, allowing the two metals to be separated by controlling pH in the classical qualitative analysis scheme.

Complex formation enhances solubility by removing a free ion from the precipitation equilibrium. Silver chloride dissolves in concentrated ammonia because silver forms the diamminesilver complex, lowering the free silver concentration so that the ion product no longer exceeds the solubility product, and the solid redissolves until the complex equilibrium is satisfied.

The reaction quotient compared to the solubility product predicts whether a precipitate forms. If the product of the actual ion concentrations exceeds the solubility product the solution is supersaturated and a solid deposits, if it equals it the solution is saturated and at equilibrium, and if it is smaller the solution is unsaturated and any solid present continues to dissolve.

Fractional precipitation of calcium and magnesium underlies water softening. Adding carbonate precipitates calcium carbonate first because of its lower solubility product, and lime addition raises the pH enough to precipitate magnesium as the hydroxide. The combined treatment removes the hardness ions responsible for scale and soap scum.

Salts whose constituent ions hydrolyse can be more soluble in acid than the solubility product alone would suggest. Calcium fluoride dissolves more readily in acidic solution because protons consume fluoride as hydrofluoric acid, depleting the free fluoride concentration and dragging the dissolution equilibrium forward until the buffered acid is exhausted.

Barium sulphate is so insoluble, with a solubility product near 1e-10, that it is administered as a radiocontrast agent despite barium ions being toxic. The free barium concentration in equilibrium with the solid is far below any harmful threshold, and excess sulphate in the formulation suppresses dissolution further through the common ion effect.

The molar solubility of a salt with formula AB2 is not simply the square root of its solubility product. If the solid dissolves to give s moles of A and 2s moles of B, the ion product is s times (2s) squared, equal to four s cubed, so the solubility is the cube root of one quarter of the solubility product.

Radioactive decay follows first-order kinetics, the number of nuclei decaying per unit time being proportional to the number present. The half-life relates to the decay constant through the natural logarithm of two divided by the constant, and after each half-life the activity falls by exactly half regardless of the starting amount, the hallmark of an exponential process.

Radiocarbon dating exploits the steady production of carbon-14 in the atmosphere and its uptake by living organisms. When an organism dies it stops exchanging carbon, and the carbon-14 decays with a half-life of 5730 years. Measuring the residual carbon-14 to carbon-12 ratio and applying the exponential decay law yields an age accurate over roughly fifty thousand years.

Alpha decay emits a helium nucleus, lowering the mass number by four and the atomic number by two. Uranium-238 decaying to thorium-234 is a classic example. The emitted alpha particle carries a discrete energy because the decay connects two definite nuclear states, and its short range in matter makes it dangerous only when an alpha emitter is ingested or inhaled.

Beta-minus decay converts a neutron into a proton, emitting an electron and an antineutrino, so the atomic number rises by one while the mass number is unchanged. Carbon-14 decays this way to nitrogen-14. Because the emitted energy is shared with the unseen antineutrino, beta particles emerge with a continuous spectrum of energies up to a sharp endpoint.

Nuclear binding energy is the energy released when nucleons assemble into a nucleus, reflected in a mass defect through the mass-energy equivalence. The binding energy per nucleon peaks near iron-56, so fusing light nuclei and splitting heavy ones both release energy, accounting for stellar fusion at one end of the curve and reactor fission at the other.

A decay series steps a heavy unstable nucleus down to a stable endpoint through successive alpha and beta emissions. The uranium-238 series passes through fourteen intermediates, including radium and radon, before terminating at stable lead-206. Within such a series a state of secular equilibrium develops in which each short-lived daughter decays as fast as it is formed.

Isotopes of an element share the same number of protons but differ in neutrons, so they are chemically nearly identical yet differ in mass and nuclear stability. Chlorine occurs as a mixture of chlorine-35 and chlorine-37 in roughly a three-to-one ratio, which is why its atomic weight on the periodic table is the non-integer value 35.45.

Electron capture occurs when a proton-rich nucleus absorbs an inner-shell electron, converting a proton to a neutron and emitting a neutrino. The vacancy left in the electron shell is filled from above, releasing a characteristic X-ray. Potassium-40 decays partly by this route to argon-40, the basis of potassium-argon dating of volcanic rocks.

Induced nuclear fission of uranium-235 occurs when the nucleus absorbs a slow neutron, becomes unstable, and splits into two medium-mass fragments while releasing two or three neutrons. Those neutrons can trigger further fissions, and when the multiplication factor reaches one a self-sustaining chain reaction is established, the controllable basis of nuclear power generation.

A radioactive tracer is an isotope substituted into a molecule so that its progress can be followed by the radiation it emits. Phosphorus-32 incorporated into a nucleotide tags it without altering its chemistry, and gamma-emitting technetium-99m introduced into the body localises in tissues of interest, the workhorse of diagnostic nuclear medicine imaging.

Huckel's rule identifies a planar, fully conjugated, monocyclic ring as aromatic when it holds 4n+2 pi electrons. Benzene with six pi electrons satisfies the count, as do the cyclopentadienyl anion and the cycloheptatrienyl cation, each contributing six electrons to a continuous overlapping array of parallel p orbitals encircling the ring.

Antiaromatic rings carrying 4n pi electrons are destabilised relative to an open-chain reference. Cyclobutadiene with four pi electrons is so unstable that it dimerises rapidly even at low temperature, and it distorts to a rectangular geometry that breaks the degeneracy of its highest occupied orbitals to avoid an open-shell triplet.

The aromatic stabilisation of benzene is quantified by comparing its experimental heat of hydrogenation with three times that of cyclohexene. The measured value falls short of the prediction by roughly 150 kilojoules per mole, and this resonance energy reflects the extra stability conferred by delocalising the six pi electrons over all six carbon atoms.

Conjugation lowers the energy of a pi system by letting electron density spread over adjacent p orbitals. In 1,3-butadiene both the s-cis and s-trans conformers retain conjugation, and the central carbon-carbon single bond is shorter than an ordinary single bond because of the partial double-bond character contributed by the delocalised framework.

A diatropic ring current circulates in an aromatic molecule when an external magnetic field induces motion of the delocalised electrons. The induced field shields protons inside the ring and deshields those on the periphery, explaining why benzene hydrogens resonate near 7.3 parts per million while inner protons of larger annulenes appear at strongly negative shifts.

Pyridine is aromatic because its nitrogen contributes one electron to the pi sextet while its lone pair occupies an sp2 orbital in the ring plane, free for protonation and metal coordination. Pyrrole is also aromatic, but its nitrogen donates both lone-pair electrons into the pi system, leaving the molecule a weak base and a reactive substrate toward electrophiles.

Naphthalene, anthracene, and phenanthrene are polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons whose fused rings share pi electrons across the framework. The resonance energy per ring falls with increasing linear fusion, so the central ring of anthracene is the most reactive site and readily undergoes Diels-Alder addition across its 9 and 10 positions while the outer rings stay aromatic.

Cross-conjugation occurs when three unsaturated groups branch from a central atom so that conjugation extends along any two paths but never all three at once. Divinyl ketone exemplifies the pattern, and the electronic communication between its two vinyl groups is attenuated relative to a linearly conjugated dienone, altering both ultraviolet absorption and reactivity.

The tropylium cation is an aromatic seven-membered ring carrying a single positive charge and six pi electrons delocalised over all seven carbons. Its stability lets it form spontaneously when cycloheptatriene loses hydride, and the aromatic character also explains the prominent mass-spectral fragment at mass-to-charge 91 that arises when benzylic ions rearrange to tropylium.

Extending conjugation shifts ultraviolet-visible absorption toward longer wavelength because each added double bond raises the energy of the highest occupied orbital and lowers the lowest unoccupied orbital, narrowing the gap. Beta-carotene, with eleven conjugated double bonds, absorbs blue-green light near 450 nanometres and consequently appears orange to the eye.

Deprotonation of a ketone at the alpha carbon by a strong, non-nucleophilic base such as lithium diisopropylamide generates an enolate whose negative charge is delocalised onto oxygen. Performing the deprotonation cold under kinetic control favours the less substituted enolate, because the base abstracts the more accessible proton faster than it can reach equilibrium.

Keto-enol tautomerism interconverts a carbonyl compound and its enol by migration of an alpha hydrogen to oxygen and a shift of the double bond. For simple ketones the keto form dominates overwhelmingly, but in 1,3-dicarbonyl compounds the enol is stabilised by conjugation and an intramolecular hydrogen bond, and acetylacetone exists as roughly four parts enol in the neat liquid.

The Michael addition delivers a stabilised carbon nucleophile to the beta carbon of an alpha,beta-unsaturated carbonyl compound. The enolate of a 1,3-dicarbonyl attacks in conjugate fashion, and the resulting enolate is protonated on workup. The reaction builds carbon-carbon bonds under mild basic conditions and forms the first stage of the Robinson annulation sequence.

The haloform reaction exhaustively halogenates the methyl group of a methyl ketone because each new halogen raises the acidity of the remaining alpha protons. The trihalomethyl ketone is then cleaved by hydroxide into a carboxylate and a haloform, and the appearance of yellow iodoform from a methyl ketone treated with iodine and base is a classic qualitative test.

The Mannich reaction couples an enolisable carbonyl compound, formaldehyde, and a secondary amine to install an aminomethyl group at the alpha carbon. The amine and aldehyde first condense to an iminium ion, which the enol of the ketone then attacks. The beta-amino ketone product can eliminate to an enone, providing a route to alpha-methylene carbonyl compounds.

Alkylation of the acetoacetic ester enolate followed by acid hydrolysis and decarboxylation provides a general synthesis of substituted methyl ketones. The active methylene flanked by two carbonyls is acidic enough for mild bases, and once the carbon skeleton is built the beta-keto acid loses carbon dioxide on heating through a cyclic six-membered transition state.

An enamine, formed by condensing a secondary amine with a ketone, behaves as a neutral nucleophile equivalent to an enolate. The nitrogen lone pair pushes electron density onto the alpha carbon, which attacks alkyl halides or Michael acceptors. Hydrolysis of the iminium product regenerates the carbonyl, completing the Stork enamine alkylation without strongly basic conditions.

Alpha-halogenation of a ketone under acidic conditions proceeds through the enol, which attacks the halogen and installs a single halogen at the alpha carbon. Unlike the base-promoted reaction, the acidic version stops cleanly at monohalogenation because the electron-withdrawing halogen retards formation of a second enol, an electronic brake the base-promoted route lacks.

The Knoevenagel condensation joins an aldehyde with an active methylene compound such as malonic ester under amine catalysis. The amine forms an iminium with the aldehyde and also deprotonates the acidic methylene, and the resulting carbanion adds and then eliminates water to give an alkene conjugated with the two electron-withdrawing groups.

The Baeyer-Villiger oxidation inserts an oxygen atom between the carbonyl carbon and an adjacent carbon of a ketone, converting it to an ester. A peroxyacid adds to the carbonyl to give a tetrahedral Criegee intermediate, and the more substituted group migrates to oxygen with retention of configuration as the oxygen-oxygen bond breaks.

Diborane adopts a structure with two bridging hydrogen atoms held by three-centre two-electron bonds, in which a single pair of electrons binds three atoms across a banana-shaped orbital. The molecule is electron-deficient, having too few valence electrons for ordinary two-centre bonds, which explains its bridged geometry and high reactivity toward Lewis bases.

The thermal stability of the group 14 hydrides falls sharply down the group as the element-hydrogen bond weakens. Methane endures several hundred degrees, silane ignites in air, germane decomposes more readily still, and stannane and plumbane survive only fleetingly, a trend tracing to the diminishing orbital overlap as the central atom grows larger.
