Lithium aluminium hydride is a powerful nucleophilic hydride source that reduces esters, carboxylic acids, amides, and nitriles, delivering hydride to electrophilic carbon. Sodium borohydride is milder, reducing aldehydes and ketones but leaving esters untouched, a difference reflecting the greater polarity and weaker metal-hydrogen bond of the aluminium reagent.

Phosphine is a far weaker base than ammonia because the larger phosphorus atom holds its lone pair in a more diffuse orbital with poor overlap toward an incoming proton. The bond angle in phosphine, near 93 degrees, is much smaller than in ammonia, reflecting reduced hybridisation and lone-pair character at the larger central atom.

Silane reacts with water only when catalysed by trace base, unlike the inert methane, because silicon can expand its coordination sphere and accept nucleophilic attack at the central atom. The hydrolysis liberates hydrogen and forms silica gel, and the susceptibility of the silicon-hydrogen bond underlies the use of silanes as reducing agents.

Borohydride and aluminohydride anions are tetrahedral with four equivalent element-hydrogen bonds, isoelectronic with methane and the ammonium ion. The hydridic hydrogen carries partial negative charge, opposite in polarity to the protic hydrogen of water, so combining a hydride with a proton source liberates molecular hydrogen in a vigorous union of opposite hydrogen oxidation states.

Hydrazine, formally a hydride of nitrogen with an N-N single bond, is a powerful reducing agent and rocket propellant. Its decomposition to nitrogen, ammonia, and hydrogen is strongly exothermic, and catalytic decomposition over iridium furnishes a monopropellant thruster gas. The molecule adopts a gauche conformation that minimises lone-pair repulsion across the central bond.

The boron hydrides form an extensive series of cluster compounds whose structures Wade's rules rationalise by counting skeletal electron pairs. A closo cluster with n vertices has n plus one skeletal pairs, a nido cluster has n plus two, and an arachno cluster has n plus three, each successive class derived by stripping a vertex from the parent deltahedron.

Hydrogen fluoride forms zigzag hydrogen-bonded chains in the liquid and retains polymeric association even in the vapour, where the average aggregate approaches a hexamer near the boiling point. The strong hydrogen bonding and high polarity of the H-F bond make anhydrous hydrogen fluoride a weakly conducting, strongly self-ionising solvent quite unlike the other hydrogen halides.

Ammonia, water, and hydrogen fluoride show anomalously high boiling points among the hydrides of their groups because hydrogen bonding links the molecules through the lone pairs of the electronegative central atom. The hydrides of the heavier congeners lack this association and follow the expected trend of rising boiling point with molar mass.

The Sharpless epoxidation converts an allylic alcohol into a chiral epoxide using titanium tetraisopropoxide, tert-butyl hydroperoxide, and a single enantiomer of diethyl tartrate. The tartrate ligand sets the facial selectivity, and a simple mnemonic predicts which enantiomer of epoxide forms from a given tartrate, delivering enantiomeric excesses routinely above 90 percent.

Asymmetric hydrogenation with a rhodium complex bearing a chiral bisphosphine ligand reduces a prochiral enamide to a single enantiomer of an amino acid derivative. The chiral pocket discriminates between the two faces of the bound alkene, and the major enantiomer often arises from the less stable diastereomeric catalyst-substrate complex because it reacts faster.

Organocatalysis by the amino acid proline accelerates the asymmetric aldol reaction through an enamine intermediate. The carboxylic acid of proline directs the incoming aldehyde by hydrogen bonding while the pyrrolidine ring forms the nucleophilic enamine, and the rigid bicyclic transition state delivers the new stereocentre with high enantioselectivity under mild metal-free conditions.

A chiral auxiliary is a removable enantiopure group attached to a substrate to bias the stereochemistry of a subsequent reaction. The Evans oxazolidinone directs alkylation and aldol reactions of the attached acyl group with high diastereoselectivity, and after the new stereocentre is set the auxiliary is cleaved and recovered for reuse.

Enantiomeric excess measures the optical purity of a sample as the difference between the mole fractions of the two enantiomers, equivalent to the percentage of one enantiomer in excess of the racemate. A reaction giving 95 percent excess produces a 97.5 to 2.5 ratio of enantiomers, and chiral chromatography or NMR with a shift reagent quantifies the value directly.

Kinetic resolution exploits the unequal reaction rates of two enantiomers with a chiral catalyst or reagent. A lipase that acylates one enantiomer of a racemic alcohol much faster than the other leaves the slow enantiomer unreacted, so partial conversion yields both the enantiopure ester and the enantiopure recovered alcohol at the cost of half the material.

The asymmetric dihydroxylation of an alkene with osmium tetroxide and a cinchona alkaloid ligand installs two adjacent hydroxyl groups on a single face with predictable absolute configuration. The two pseudoenantiomeric ligands, derived from dihydroquinine and dihydroquinidine, deliver the diol to opposite faces, and a sketched mnemonic quadrant predicts which enantiomer results.

Chiral amplification occurs when a small initial enantiomeric excess in a catalyst is magnified into a much larger excess in the product. In the Soai autocatalytic reaction the chiral product itself catalyses its own formation, and a nonlinear relationship between catalyst and product purity, arising from the formation of inactive heterochiral dimers, drives the system toward homochirality.

The Corey-Bakshi-Shibata reduction uses a chiral oxazaborolidine catalyst to reduce a prochiral ketone to a secondary alcohol of defined configuration. Borane coordinates to the catalyst nitrogen while the ketone binds to boron, and the rigid six-membered transition state transfers hydride to one face selectively, giving enantiomeric excesses commonly exceeding 95 percent.

Dynamic kinetic resolution overcomes the fifty percent yield ceiling of ordinary kinetic resolution by racemising the slow-reacting enantiomer in situ. A ruthenium catalyst continuously interconverts the two enantiomers of a substrate while a lipase selectively acylates one of them, funnelling the entire racemate toward a single enantiopure product in high yield.

Pyrrole, furan, and thiophene are five-membered aromatic heterocycles in which the heteroatom donates a lone pair into the pi sextet. Their reactivity toward electrophilic substitution follows the order pyrrole greater than furan greater than thiophene, mirroring how readily each heteroatom shares its electrons, and substitution occurs preferentially at the 2-position.

Pyridine undergoes electrophilic substitution sluggishly and at the 3-position because the electronegative nitrogen withdraws electron density and destabilises the intermediates leading to 2- and 4-substitution. Nucleophilic substitution, by contrast, occurs readily at the 2- and 4-positions, where the developing negative charge is stabilised on nitrogen.

The Paal-Knorr synthesis builds five-membered heterocycles from 1,4-dicarbonyl compounds. Treatment with a primary amine yields a pyrrole, with phosphorus pentasulfide a thiophene, and with acid a furan, in each case through cyclisation and loss of water. The reaction is a reliable route to substituted azoles when the dicarbonyl precursor is accessible.

Imidazole is a five-membered ring with two nitrogen atoms of differing character: one pyrrole-type that donates its lone pair to the aromatic sextet and one pyridine-type that retains a basic lone pair in the plane. Rapid tautomeric exchange of the N-H proton between the two nitrogens makes the ring positions equivalent on the NMR timescale at room temperature.

Indole fuses a benzene ring to a pyrrole and undergoes electrophilic substitution at the 3-position, since attack there gives an intermediate that preserves the benzenoid aromaticity. The Fischer indole synthesis assembles the ring from an arylhydrazine and a ketone through a 3,3-sigmatropic rearrangement followed by loss of ammonia and ring closure.

Pyrimidine carries two nitrogen atoms at the 1- and 3-positions of a six-membered aromatic ring and is strongly deactivated toward electrophiles. The ring forms the core of the nucleobases cytosine, thymine, and uracil, and its electron-poor character allows nucleophilic displacement of leaving groups at the 2-, 4-, and 6-positions in many pharmaceutical syntheses.

Furan behaves as a reactive diene in the Diels-Alder reaction, adding to dienophiles such as maleic anhydride to give an oxabicyclic adduct. The aromatic stabilisation of furan is modest, so it sacrifices aromaticity readily, and the cycloaddition is often reversible, with the retro reaction releasing furan again on gentle heating.

Quinoline and isoquinoline are benzopyridines differing in the position of the ring nitrogen. The Skraup synthesis constructs quinoline by condensing aniline with glycerol, which dehydrates to acrolein in situ, followed by conjugate addition, cyclisation, and oxidation. A mild oxidant such as nitrobenzene aromatises the dihydro intermediate to the final ring.

Epoxides are three-membered oxygen heterocycles whose ring strain near 114 kilojoules per mole makes them highly reactive toward nucleophiles. Under basic conditions the nucleophile attacks the less hindered carbon with inversion, while under acidic conditions protonation of the oxygen shifts attack toward the more substituted carbon that better supports positive charge.

Aziridines, the nitrogen analogues of epoxides, retain substantial ring strain and open with nucleophiles when the nitrogen bears an electron-withdrawing activating group. The barrier to nitrogen inversion is raised by the ring constraint, so an aziridine with three different substituents on a stereogenic nitrogen can in favourable cases be resolved into separable invertomers.

A carbocation rearranges when a hydrogen or alkyl group migrates from an adjacent carbon to convert a less stable cation into a more stable one. A secondary carbocation flanked by a quaternary carbon undergoes a 1,2-methyl shift to become a tertiary cation, and the migrating group moves with its bonding electron pair so that no separate intermediate forms.

The pinacol rearrangement converts a 1,2-diol into a ketone under acid catalysis. Protonation and loss of one hydroxyl generate a carbocation, and a group from the carbon bearing the remaining hydroxyl migrates to the cationic centre. The oxygen lone pair then expels a proton to form the carbonyl, with the most stabilised cation dictating which hydroxyl departs.

Hydride shifts allow a carbocation to relocate along a carbon chain, and a cascade of successive 1,2-hydride shifts can move positive charge several carbons from its origin. Each shift is favoured only if it produces a cation of equal or greater stability, so the charge migrates toward more substituted positions and toward sites stabilised by adjacent heteroatoms.

Neighbouring-group participation by a beta heteroatom or pi bond stabilises a developing carbocation by bridging across the cationic centre. The bridged phenonium and bromonium ions formed in this way distribute the positive charge over two carbons, lower the energy of the intermediate, and dictate the stereochemistry of the product by controlling which face the nucleophile attacks.

The Wagner-Meerwein rearrangement is a 1,2-shift of an alkyl or aryl group within a carbocation, central to the chemistry of bicyclic terpenes. The rearrangement of the bornyl cation to the camphene framework proceeds through skeletal reorganisation, and the strained ring systems of natural monoterpenes provide ample thermodynamic driving force for such migrations.

Solvolysis of a neopentyl substrate is anomalously slow and gives a rearranged product because the primary carbocation that would form is too unstable. Instead a concerted ionisation with simultaneous methyl migration generates the tertiary cation directly, so the rate-determining step bypasses the primary cation entirely while delivering a tert-amyl product.

Allylic carbocations are stabilised by resonance that delocalises the positive charge over two terminal carbons. A nucleophile may then attack either terminus, giving products of direct and of allylic-shifted substitution. The ratio of the two depends on the relative stability and steric accessibility of the two possible attack sites within the delocalised cation.

The non-classical 2-norbornyl cation distributes its positive charge over three carbon atoms through a bridged sigma bond rather than residing on a single centre. The cation displays extraordinary stability and stereospecific reactivity, and decades of debate over its classical versus non-classical structure were ultimately resolved in favour of the symmetric bridged description by low-temperature spectroscopy.

Ring expansion of a strained cyclic carbocation relieves angle strain by migration of a ring bond to the cationic carbon. A cyclobutylmethyl cation rearranges to the less strained cyclopentyl cation, and a cyclopropylcarbinyl cation enjoys special stabilisation through donation from the bent ring bonds before ring-opening to a homoallyl product.

In a Friedel-Crafts alkylation the electrophile is a carbocation generated from an alkyl halide and a Lewis acid, and it can rearrange before attacking the arene. Alkylation with 1-chloropropane yields chiefly isopropylbenzene because the primary cation undergoes a hydride shift to the more stable secondary cation faster than it reacts with benzene.

The carbon-fluorine bond is the strongest single bond carbon forms, with a dissociation energy near 480 kilojoules per mole, owing to the small size of fluorine and the strong electrostatic component of the highly polar bond. This strength confers exceptional thermal and chemical stability on perfluorinated compounds and underlies the inertness of fully fluorinated materials.

Replacing a hydrogen with fluorine in a drug candidate often blocks oxidative metabolism at that position because the carbon-fluorine bond resists cleavage by cytochrome enzymes. The small steric demand of fluorine, comparable to hydrogen, lets the substitution proceed without major conformational disruption while modulating the molecule's lipophilicity and acidity.

Deoxofluorination reagents such as diethylaminosulfur trifluoride convert a hydroxyl group into a fluoride with inversion of configuration at carbon. The reagent first activates the oxygen as a leaving group, and fluoride then displaces it through a backside attack, providing a direct route to secondary alkyl fluorides from readily available alcohols.

Trifluoromethyl groups withdraw electron density strongly through induction, lowering the basicity of nearby amines and raising the acidity of nearby alcohols and acids. Trifluoroacetic acid is roughly ten thousand times stronger than acetic acid because the three fluorines stabilise the carboxylate anion by dispersing its negative charge through the sigma framework.

Fluorine-18 is a positron-emitting isotope incorporated into tracers for positron emission tomography. The radiolabelled glucose analogue fluorodeoxyglucose accumulates in metabolically active tissue and is trapped after phosphorylation. The short half-life near 110 minutes demands rapid synthesis and prompt imaging once the labelled molecule is prepared.

Perfluorocarbon liquids dissolve large volumes of oxygen and carbon dioxide because the weak intermolecular forces between fluorinated chains create cavities that gases occupy readily. The same weak cohesion gives these liquids low surface tension and high density, and their chemical inertness has been explored for liquid breathing and as blood substitutes.

Electrophilic fluorinating reagents such as Selectfluor deliver a formally positive fluorine to an electron-rich substrate. The reagent transfers fluorine to enolates, electron-rich arenes, and alkenes, installing a single fluorine where a nucleophilic site can attack the weakly held fluorine atom bound to a positively charged nitrogen.

The high electronegativity of fluorine makes a fluorinated alkyl chain both hydrophobic and lipophobic, so perfluorinated surfactants segregate to interfaces more strongly than hydrocarbon analogues. This dual phobicity drives fluorous-phase separation, in which a heavily fluorinated molecule partitions selectively into a perfluorocarbon solvent immiscible with both water and ordinary organic solvents.

Hydrofluorination of an alkyne with a gold catalyst adds hydrogen and fluorine across the triple bond to give a vinyl fluoride. The metal activates the alkyne toward attack by a fluoride source, and the regiochemistry follows Markovnikov selectivity, placing the fluorine on the more substituted carbon of the resulting alkene.

Fluorine-19 nuclear magnetic resonance is highly sensitive because the isotope is the only naturally occurring one and has a spin of one half. The enormous range of fluorine chemical shifts, spanning several hundred parts per million, makes the technique exquisitely responsive to small changes in chemical environment and a powerful probe of binding and conformation in fluorinated molecules.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: A peptide bond forms by condensation of the carboxyl group of one amino acid with the amino group of another, expelling water. The reaction is thermodynamically unfavourable in aqueous solution, so synthesis activates the carboxyl as a reactive ester or anhydride first, and the resulting amide adopts a planar trans geometry stabilised by partial double-bond character.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Solid-phase peptide synthesis anchors the growing chain to an insoluble resin so that excess reagents and byproducts are washed away after each coupling. The chain is extended from the carboxyl terminus toward the amino terminus through repeated cycles of deprotection and coupling, and the finished peptide is cleaved from the resin with strong acid at the end.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: The fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl group protects the amino terminus during peptide synthesis and is removed under mild basic conditions with piperidine, which abstracts a fluorenyl proton and triggers an elimination releasing carbon dioxide and dibenzofulvene. Its base-lability makes it orthogonal to the acid-labile side-chain protecting groups used alongside it.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Carbodiimide coupling reagents activate a carboxylic acid by forming an O-acylisourea that is readily attacked by an amine. To suppress racemisation and the unproductive rearrangement to an unreactive N-acylurea, an additive such as hydroxybenzotriazole intercepts the activated intermediate and forms a less epimerising active ester before the amine couples.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Orthogonal protection uses two or more protecting groups removable under mutually independent conditions, so each can be cleaved without disturbing the others. A peptide synthesis combining a base-labile amino protector with an acid-labile carboxyl protector lets the chemist unmask one terminus at a time and direct the order of bond formation precisely.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: The tert-butoxycarbonyl group shields an amine as a carbamate and is removed by treatment with trifluoroacetic acid, which protonates the carbonyl oxygen and triggers loss of a stable tert-butyl cation followed by decarboxylation. Its acid-lability complements the base-labile fluorenylmethyloxycarbonyl group in two-dimensional protection schemes.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Native chemical ligation joins two unprotected peptide fragments by reacting a carboxyl-terminal thioester with an amino-terminal cysteine. A reversible transthioesterification first links the fragments, and a spontaneous intramolecular acyl shift then converts the thioester into a stable peptide bond, enabling the assembly of full-length proteins from synthetic pieces.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Racemisation during peptide coupling threatens the stereochemical integrity of each amino acid. An activated carboxyl can cyclise to an oxazolone whose alpha proton is acidic enough to be removed, scrambling the stereocentre. Coupling at low temperature with minimal base and an azabenzotriazole additive keeps epimerisation below one percent per coupling.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Benzyl ethers and esters protect hydroxyl and carboxyl groups and are cleaved by catalytic hydrogenolysis over palladium, which cleaves the benzylic carbon-oxygen bond and releases toluene. Because hydrogenolysis proceeds under neutral conditions, the benzyl group is orthogonal to acid- and base-labile protectors and survives both acidic and basic deprotection steps.

subtopic: peptide bond formation and protecting groups
sentence: Aspartimide formation is a notorious side reaction in which the side-chain carbonyl of an aspartate residue is attacked by the backbone amide nitrogen of the following residue, forming a cyclic imide. The imide can then open to either the desired alpha-peptide or an unwanted beta-peptide, and bulky aspartate protecting groups are chosen specifically to suppress the cyclisation.

Terpenes are built from five-carbon isoprene units assembled head to tail. The biological isoprene equivalents are isopentenyl pyrophosphate and its isomer dimethylallyl pyrophosphate, which condense to give the ten-carbon geranyl pyrophosphate, the universal precursor of the monoterpenes, with each elongation adding another five-carbon unit.

Chain elongation in terpene biosynthesis proceeds by ionisation of the pyrophosphate leaving group to form an allylic carbocation, which is attacked by the terminal double bond of isopentenyl pyrophosphate. Loss of a proton regenerates a double bond, and repeated cycles extend the chain to geranyl, farnesyl, and geranylgeranyl pyrophosphates of progressively greater length.

Cyclisation of farnesyl pyrophosphate generates the bewildering diversity of sesquiterpene skeletons. Ionisation produces a fifteen-carbon allylic cation that folds and is captured by an internal double bond, and the resulting new carbocation can undergo hydride shifts, methyl migrations, and further ring closures before a final deprotonation fixes the carbon framework.

Squalene, a thirty-carbon triterpene, is formed by reductive tail-to-tail coupling of two molecules of farnesyl pyrophosphate. Its enzymatic epoxidation gives 2,3-oxidosqualene, which undergoes a remarkable cation-driven polycyclisation cascade that forms four rings in a single concerted sequence, the biosynthetic origin of lanosterol and ultimately of cholesterol.

The isoprene rule, recognised by Wallach and refined by Ruzicka, observes that terpene carbon skeletons can be divided into isoprene units joined in a regular head-to-tail pattern. The biogenetic isoprene rule extended the idea by proposing that the skeletons arise from cyclisation and rearrangement of a small number of acyclic polyprenyl precursors.

Monoterpene cyclases convert geranyl pyrophosphate into cyclic products by first isomerising it to linalyl pyrophosphate, whose freely rotating bond allows the chain to coil. Ionisation then yields a cyclohexenyl cation that is quenched in different ways, producing limonene, alpha-pinene, or camphene depending on how the enzyme channels the reactive intermediate.

The mevalonate pathway supplies isopentenyl pyrophosphate in animals and fungi, beginning with condensation of three acetyl-CoA units into hydroxymethylglutaryl-CoA. Reduction to mevalonate, two phosphorylations, and a decarboxylative elimination then deliver the activated five-carbon building block from which all isoprenoids in those organisms ultimately descend.

Carotenoids are forty-carbon tetraterpenes formed by tail-to-tail coupling of two geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate molecules into phytoene. A sequence of desaturations introduces the extended conjugated polyene that absorbs visible light, and cyclisation of the chain ends produces the beta-ionone rings found in beta-carotene and many related pigments.

The non-mevalonate, or methylerythritol phosphate, pathway operates in plant plastids and many bacteria, building isopentenyl pyrophosphate from pyruvate and glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate rather than from acetyl-CoA. Its absence in humans makes the enzymes of this route attractive targets for antimalarial and antibacterial drug design.

Diterpene biosynthesis from geranylgeranyl pyrophosphate frequently proceeds through a two-stage cyclisation. A protonation-initiated cyclisation first forms a bicyclic labdane-type cation, and a separate ionisation-driven cyclisation then closes additional rings, a strategy that gives rise to the complex polycyclic skeletons of the gibberellin plant hormones and the taxane diterpenes.

A radical chain reaction comprises three phases: initiation generates radicals by homolytic bond cleavage, propagation consumes one radical and produces another so the chain is self-sustaining, and termination destroys radicals by combination or disproportionation. The chain length, the average number of propagation cycles per initiation event, can reach thousands when termination is slow.

Allylic bromination with N-bromosuccinimide proceeds by a radical chain in which the succinimide reagent maintains a low, steady concentration of molecular bromine. The low bromine concentration favours hydrogen abstraction at the weak allylic C-H bond over addition across the double bond, so substitution rather than addition becomes the dominant pathway.

Autoxidation of an organic substrate by atmospheric oxygen is a radical chain in which a carbon radical adds oxygen to form a peroxyl radical, which abstracts a hydrogen to give a hydroperoxide and a new carbon radical. The accumulation of hydroperoxides explains the gradual rancidification of fats and the formation of explosive peroxides in aged ethers.

Antioxidants interrupt radical chains by donating a hydrogen atom to a chain-carrying radical and forming a stabilised radical too unreactive to continue propagation. Phenolic antioxidants such as butylated hydroxytoluene give a resonance-delocalised phenoxyl radical, which terminates the chain rather than abstracting another hydrogen from the substrate.

The anti-Markovnikov addition of hydrogen bromide to an alkene proceeds when peroxides are present, switching the mechanism from ionic to radical. A bromine atom adds to the less hindered carbon to give the more stable secondary radical, which then abstracts hydrogen from hydrogen bromide, so the bromine ends up on the less substituted carbon.

Radical polymerisation of an alkene monomer extends a chain by repeated addition of the carbon radical to the next monomer's double bond. The reactive chain end propagates until two growing radicals meet and terminate, and chain transfer to solvent or monomer caps the molecular weight while starting a fresh chain elsewhere.

Azobisisobutyronitrile is a common radical initiator that decomposes on gentle heating, expelling a molecule of nitrogen and releasing two carbon-centred radicals. The loss of stable dinitrogen provides the thermodynamic driving force, and the decomposition rate, with a convenient half-life near ten hours at 65 degrees Celsius, makes the reagent a controllable radical source.

The radical chlorination of methane shows poor selectivity because the chlorine atom is highly reactive and abstracts hydrogen with a low activation barrier, so even slightly stronger bonds are attacked at competitive rates. Bromination is far more selective because the bromine atom is less reactive, giving a later transition state that discriminates sharply among C-H bond strengths.

The Barton-McCombie deoxygenation removes a secondary hydroxyl group through a radical chain. The alcohol is first converted to a thiocarbonyl derivative, a tributyltin radical adds to the thiocarbonyl sulfur, and the resulting carbon radical abstracts hydrogen from tin hydride, replacing the oxygen functionality with hydrogen under mild neutral conditions.

Radical cyclisation of a hex-5-enyl radical favours the five-membered ring over the six-membered ring, contrary to thermodynamic stability. The Baldwin rules and stereoelectronic analysis of the transition state show that the chair-like arrangement for 5-exo-trig closure aligns the radical with the alkene pi system more effectively than the 6-endo alternative.

Hess's law states that the enthalpy change of a reaction is independent of the path taken, because enthalpy is a state function. The enthalpy of a target reaction can therefore be assembled by adding the enthalpies of a sequence of known reactions that sum to it, reversing any reaction's sign when its direction is flipped.

A bomb calorimeter measures the heat of combustion at constant volume by igniting a sample in excess oxygen inside a sealed steel vessel immersed in water. The temperature rise of the water and the calorimeter, multiplied by the heat capacity of the assembly, gives the internal energy change, which is converted to enthalpy by adding the work term for the change in moles of gas.

The standard enthalpy of formation is the enthalpy change when one mole of a compound forms from its elements in their reference states. The enthalpy of any reaction equals the sum of the formation enthalpies of the products minus that of the reactants, since the elemental reference states cancel and define the zero of the formation scale.

Bond enthalpies provide an estimate of reaction enthalpy by treating the process as breaking all the bonds in the reactants and forming all the bonds in the products. The reaction enthalpy approximates the sum of bond enthalpies broken minus the sum of bond enthalpies formed, although the values are averages and the estimate carries an uncertainty of tens of kilojoules.

Calorimetry at constant pressure, as in a simple coffee-cup apparatus, measures heat directly as the enthalpy change of the reaction. The heat absorbed or released equals the mass of solution times its specific heat times the temperature change, and dividing by the moles of limiting reagent gives the molar enthalpy of the process.

The enthalpy of solution is the heat change when a solute dissolves, equal to the lattice enthalpy that must be supplied to separate the ions plus the hydration enthalpy released as the ions are surrounded by water. When hydration outweighs the lattice term the dissolution is exothermic, and when the lattice term dominates the solution cools.

The temperature dependence of a reaction enthalpy follows Kirchhoff's law, which states that the rate of change of enthalpy with temperature equals the difference in heat capacity between products and reactants. Integrating this relation lets a reaction enthalpy measured at one temperature be corrected to another, provided the heat capacities are known over the range.

Differential scanning calorimetry measures the heat flow into a sample relative to a reference as both are heated at a controlled rate. Endothermic events such as melting appear as peaks absorbing heat, exothermic events such as crystallisation appear as peaks releasing it, and the area under each peak yields the enthalpy of the transition.

The enthalpy of neutralisation of a strong acid by a strong base is nearly constant at about minus 57 kilojoules per mole because the net reaction is always the formation of water from hydronium and hydroxide ions. Weak acids give smaller magnitudes because energy is absorbed to complete their dissociation before neutralisation.

The heat capacity of a calorimeter is found by a calibration run in which a known quantity of heat, often supplied electrically or by burning a standard such as benzoic acid, raises the temperature by a measured amount. Dividing the known heat by the temperature rise gives the calorimeter constant used to interpret subsequent measurements.

Polar protic solvents stabilise the transition state of an SN1 reaction by solvating the developing carbocation and the departing anion through hydrogen bonding and dipole interactions. The same solvents retard SN2 reactions because they cage the nucleophile in a hydrogen-bonded shell that must be partly stripped away before the nucleophile can attack.

Polar aprotic solvents such as dimethyl sulfoxide and dimethylformamide accelerate SN2 reactions dramatically. They solvate cations strongly through their negative dipole ends but cannot hydrogen-bond to anions, leaving the nucleophile poorly solvated and therefore far more reactive than the same anion in water or an alcohol.

The reaction field of a polar solvent stabilises a polar transition state in proportion to the change in dipole moment along the reaction coordinate. A reaction in which charge is created or separated speeds up in a more polar solvent, while a reaction in which charge is destroyed or dispersed slows down, a pattern captured by Hughes-Ingold solvent rules.

Solvatochromic dyes report solvent polarity through a shift in their absorption maximum, since the energy gap between ground and excited states depends on how each is stabilised by the surrounding medium. The Reichardt betaine dye gives the empirical normalised polarity scale, ranking solvents by the wavenumber of its strongly solvent-dependent charge-transfer band.

The cage effect describes how solvent molecules surround a pair of freshly formed radicals and hold them together long enough for some to recombine before they can diffuse apart. A more viscous solvent strengthens the cage, raising the fraction of geminate recombination and lowering the yield of free radicals available for productive chain chemistry.

Specific solvation through hydrogen bonding can override bulk polarity. Fluoride ion, a feeble nucleophile in water because it is tightly hydrogen-bonded, becomes a powerful nucleophile and base in dimethyl sulfoxide where no such bonding occurs. The naked anion liberated from its solvation shell expresses its full intrinsic reactivity.

Solvent polarity shifts the position of tautomeric and conformational equilibria. The enol content of a 1,3-dicarbonyl compound rises in non-polar solvents that favour the intramolecularly hydrogen-bonded enol and falls in polar solvents that compete for the carbonyl oxygens and stabilise the more polar diketo form instead.

Ionic liquids, salts molten near room temperature, serve as highly polar yet non-volatile solvents whose properties can be tuned by pairing different cations and anions. Their negligible vapour pressure and ability to dissolve both organic and inorganic species make them attractive media for reactions where solvent loss and high polarity both matter.

The Grunwald-Winstein equation correlates solvolysis rates with solvent ionising power through a linear free-energy relationship. The logarithm of the rate ratio relative to a standard solvent equals a substrate-specific sensitivity parameter multiplied by the solvent ionising power, and the slope reveals how much positive charge develops in the rate-determining step.

Hydrophobic effects can accelerate reactions in water by forcing non-polar reactants together to minimise their disruption of the hydrogen-bonded network. Diels-Alder reactions run markedly faster in aqueous suspension than in organic solvents because the diene and dienophile are pressed into proximity, and the polar transition state is further stabilised by water.

Nucleophilic acyl substitution proceeds through addition of a nucleophile to the carbonyl carbon to give a tetrahedral intermediate, followed by expulsion of the leaving group to restore the carbonyl. The net result is replacement of one group at the acyl carbon, distinguishing the reaction from the simple addition seen with aldehydes and ketones.

The reactivity of carboxylic acid derivatives toward nucleophilic acyl substitution follows the order acyl chloride greater than anhydride greater than ester greater than amide. The order tracks the leaving-group ability and the degree to which the heteroatom donates electron density into the carbonyl, since better donation deactivates the carbon and a better leaving group accelerates collapse of the tetrahedral intermediate.

Fischer esterification couples a carboxylic acid and an alcohol under acid catalysis to give an ester and water. Every step is reversible, so the equilibrium is driven toward ester by using an excess of one reactant or by removing water. Isotopic labelling shows that the ester oxygen originates from the alcohol, not the acid.

Saponification hydrolyses an ester under basic conditions to a carboxylate salt and an alcohol. Hydroxide adds to the carbonyl, the tetrahedral intermediate ejects the alkoxide, and the resulting carboxylic acid is immediately deprotonated by the alkoxide. This final irreversible deprotonation makes basic hydrolysis effectively one-way, unlike the reversible acid-catalysed reaction.

Amides are the least reactive carboxylic acid derivatives because the nitrogen lone pair is strongly delocalised into the carbonyl, giving the C-N bond substantial double-bond character. Hydrolysis of an amide therefore requires forcing conditions, prolonged heating with strong acid or base, to overcome both the poor electrophilicity and the poor leaving-group ability of the amide nitrogen.

Acyl chlorides react vigorously with alcohols and amines because chloride is an excellent leaving group and the carbonyl carbon is strongly electrophilic. The reaction with an amine releases hydrogen chloride, so a base such as pyridine is added to neutralise the acid and prevent it from protonating and deactivating the nucleophilic amine.

Transesterification exchanges the alkoxy group of an ester for that of a different alcohol under acid or base catalysis. The mechanism is the familiar addition-elimination at the acyl carbon, and the equilibrium is shifted by supplying a large excess of the incoming alcohol or by distilling away the more volatile displaced alcohol as it forms.

A carboxylic acid is converted to an acyl chloride by reagents such as thionyl chloride or oxalyl chloride, which first transform the hydroxyl into a far better leaving group. Chloride then displaces it through the addition-elimination sequence, and the byproducts, sulfur dioxide or carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide, escape as gases that drive the reaction to completion.

Acid anhydrides acylate nucleophiles and release a carboxylic acid as the leaving group. Acetic anhydride is widely used to acetylate alcohols and amines because it is more selective and easier to handle than the corresponding acyl chloride, and the carboxylate it expels is a moderate leaving group that makes the substitution clean but not violently exothermic.

A nitrile can be viewed as the most oxidised relative of the carboxylic acid family and undergoes acyl-type chemistry after hydration. Acid- or base-catalysed addition of water to the carbon-nitrogen triple bond yields an amide, which on further hydrolysis gives the carboxylic acid, so a nitrile serves as a masked carboxyl group in synthesis.
